newsitem.title: USA: Mass evacuation leaves California towns deserted.
newsitem.headline: Mass evacuation leaves California towns deserted.

text.p: Four northern California communities resembled ghost towns on Friday after a levee holding back a swollen river broke, flooding 200 homes and forcing tens of thousands of people to flee.

Some stranded residents had to be rescued by helicopter as millions of gallons (litres) of muddy water flowed through a 200-foot (60-metre) break in the levee along the Feather River, about 50 miles (80 kms) north of Sacramento.
Up to 3,000 residents of Modesto in central California were also evacuated as the Tuolumne River burst its banks, damaging homes, local officials said.

But clear skies over much of California and the Pacific Northwest brought a respite from a week of storms that have caused floods, mudslides and power outages, killed at least 18 people and caused hundreds of millions of dollars in damage in five western states.

Rivers in northern California's wine country and in Reno, Nevada -- hard hit by floods earlier in the week -- were receding, allowing residents to begin assessing the damage and clean up mud and debris.

President Bill Clinton on Friday made federal disaster relief aid available to several areas of Nevada to help them recover from the storms. Clinton's action made federal funding available to supplement state and local recovery efforts in Douglas, Lyon, Storey and Washoe counties and in Carson City.
Authorities in California said 80,000 people had been evacuated from Yuba City, Marysville, Linda and Olivehurst along the Feather River, leaving the towns deserted.
Many residents left voluntarily over the last few days but authorities ordered tens of thousands out on Thursday night as levees showed signs of weakening and one eventually gave way.

"It's enormous. I've never experienced anything like it," Bill Harris, a spokesman for the Yuba County Office of Emergency Services, said of the huge evacuation. He said there were no reports of deaths or injuries.

Water poured through the broken levee, flooding 11 square miles (28 sq kms) of mostly farmland. About 200 homes were flooded, including a number of expensive houses near a golf course, officials said.
Residents grabbed a few belongings and left the area, mostly in their own cars, on Thursday night. They spent the night at shelters or slept in their cars at gas stations.

So far none of the four towns has been flooded, but the water was moving toward Olivehurst, Harris said. He said officials planned to use trucks to dump boulders into the gap in the levee to try to slow the escaping water.

About 6,000 evacuees packed a shelter in the nearby town of Sutter. Parents sat on canvas cots while bored children raced around. "This is kind of stressful. All I can think of is my family pictures," Florence Summers, 47, said, regretting leaving behind the photos in her Yuba City home.

On Thursday, California Gov. Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency in 25 northern California counties hit by the storms, making them eligible for state aid. Emergencies have also been declared in 24 counties in Washington state, six counties in Oregon and four in Nevada.

At Yosemite National Park, 150 miles (240 kms) southeast of San Francisco, park officials were hoping to evacuate about 900 tourists stranded since Wednesday evening when all roads out of the park valley were flooded.

They said they were reassessing an earlier plan to use military helicopters to evacuate the tourists and said receding floodwaters might allow the visitors to leave by road, which park officials were examining to see whether this would be safe.

Park spokesman Chip Jenkins said the sewer system in Yosemite Valley, where the park's headquarters and lodging are located, had been shut down, the water supply was low and power had been off and on. About 1,200 park employees and their families were also stranded in the park.
Reuters correspondent Alister Bull, vacationing at the park, said guests had been told to take one suitcase and be ready to leave.

Cleanup was under way in Reno, Nevada, hit by its worst flooding in 40 years on Thursday when the Truckee river overflowed, sweeping murky brown water through homes and businesses and forcing several casinos to close. Mud and debris littered the streets. Reno airport remained closed.
A heavy equipment operator was feared drowned on Thursday when a bank he was trying to shore up at a Nevada trailer park crumbled and he was swept away by floodwater.

A major bridge near downtown Seattle used by thousands of commuters daily was closed indefinitely after a mudslide destroyed some of its steel support columns. The slide, one of more than 100 reported within the city limits, also forced the evacuation of about a dozen homes perched on a bluff in the hard-hit Magnolia neighbourhood.
